pl-l4d30c1-d1e115.summary: States that not only coercion but also error impedes or excludes consent.

pl-l4d30c1-d1e118.summary: Distinguishes errors: of person, fortune, condition, and quality. Error of person is thinking this man is that one when he is another; of fortune, thinking a poor man rich or the reverse; of condition, thinking a slave free; of quality, thinking a bad man good.
claims: There are four kinds of error.

pl-l4d30c1-d1e134.summary: States that error of fortune and quality does not exclude marital consent, but error of condition voids it, to be treated later.
claims: Error of condition voids marriage; error of fortune or quality does not.

pl-l4d30c1-d1e137.summary: Holds that error of person also excludes marital consent: if someone seeks a noble woman and is given an ignoble one instead, there is no marriage, since he consented not to her but to the other. As one promised gold and given brass did not consent to brass, since consent is of the will, so error of person excludes consent in marriage.
claims: Consent is of the will to the intended object.

pl-l4d30c1-d1e140.summary: Objects with Jacob, who served seven years for Rachel and was given Leah: did error of person exclude marriage, since he consented not to her but to Rachel?

pl-l4d30c1-d1e144.summary: Answers that what happened there is fittingly said to have been done in mystery; and though consent did not precede, it followed; nor were they fornicators in the earlier union, since he knew her with marital affection and she rendered the debt with wifely affection, thinking herself lawfully joined by the law of the firstborn and her father's command; they are also excused since it was done by God's counsel. Even today one would be excused to whom his wife's sister, entering his bed unknown, gave herself; she would remain forever without hope of marriage, but he is excused by ignorance.
claims: Jacob's case was done in mystery, and consent followed.
Ignorance excuses intercourse with an impostor.

pl-l4d30c1-d1e153.summary: Supports this by likeness: if the devil, transforming himself into an angel of light, is believed good, the error is not dangerous.
claims: Some errors about persons are harmless.

pl-l4d30c1-d1e162.summary: Shows by likeness that the man did not consent to that woman: if a heretic, using the name of Augustine or Ambrose, invited a Catholic to follow his faith and the Catholic agreed, to what faith would he have consented? Not to the heretics' sect, but to the integrity of faith the heretic falsely claimed.
claims: Consent goes to what is intended, not to the impostor.

pl-l4d30c1-d1e165.summary: Confirms that error of fortune does not exclude consent: a woman who marries a poor man thinking him rich cannot renounce him; nor error of quality: one who marries a prostitute or a woman not a virgin, thinking her chaste or a virgin, cannot dismiss her.
claims: Error of fortune or quality does not void marriage.

pl-l4d30c1.summary: Error as well as coercion can exclude consent, though not every error. Errors may concern the person, fortune, condition, or quality. Error of fortune or quality does not exclude consent; error of condition, thinking a slave free, voids it; error of person excludes marriage, as one who sought a noble woman and was given another did not consent to her, just as one promised gold and given brass did not consent to brass. Jacob, given Leah for Rachel, was a case done in mystery, and consent followed; neither was a fornicator, acting with marital affection. As believing the devil disguised as an angel to be good is no dangerous error, and as a Catholic deceived by a heretic using Augustine's name consents to true faith, not heresy, so one deceived about the person consents to the intended person.
claims: Error of person and error of servile condition void marriage.
Error of fortune or quality does not.
Jacob's marriage to Leah was done in mystery, and consent followed.
Consent is to the intended person, not to an impostor.
